name: South Face

pitch_detail.notes: Start on the right side of the south face, above the East Nooksack Glacier, and front-point partway up the snow chute. Exit left onto a sloping ledge and change from crampons and boots to rock shoes; carrying the boots and tools up the rock makes for heavy packs.
The first rock pitch, close to a full 60 m rope, angling slightly up and left. The first several pitches pass a short overhanging bulge on the way to a large depression.
The crux: 5.10- moves with a big runout on poor rock. Protection is limited throughout the face, and this pitch is the most serious lead on it.
Easier fourth-class ground up and left into the gully/depression.
Continue left on fourth-class and low-fifth-class rock. At the end of the rope, simul-climb up and left out of the depression toward the buttress on the left-center of the face.
An exposed traverse into the heart of the buttress with moves of perhaps 5.9, on loose rock with very little protection.

Three to five pitches of mid-fifth-class climbing straight up the buttress, in places loose and dirty. Protection is sparse but adequate, and the exposure is severe. The section ends at a short downclimb of about 10 ft.
A strenuous hand crack right after the downclimb. Protection is good and plentiful, but holds break, so it feels harder than its grade.

Two or three pitches of low fifth class to the top. Staying on the buttress leads onto a small tower that needs a rappel of about 50 ft just below the summit, then easy fourth-class rock to the top. Descend by the standard north face route.

descent_text: Descend by downclimbing and rappelling the standard north face route on the front (north) side of the tower rather than retracing the South Face, then reverse the glacier approach back to camp.
approach: Approach is similar to the Beckey route via Ruth Creek and Price Lake moraine, but instead of ascending toward Price Glacier, traverse to the East Nooksack Glacier. Climb to the base of the south face (elevation approximately 6,500-7,000 feet), which rises directly above the glacier. Multiple variations exist depending on snow/ice conditions; the climb starts on the right side of the face.
overview: The rarely-climbed steep south face rises directly above the East Nooksack Glacier, presenting a much more technical alpine rock and ice route than the standard north face. A serious 12-pitch Grade V climb with poor rock quality and limited protection.
beta: The South Face is the steeper 'back side' of the tower located directly above the East Nooksack Glacier, presenting as much vertical relief as the north aspect but steeper. The route starts on the right side of the south face with front-pointing up a short couloir before transitioning to rock climbing. Pitches angle slightly left and upward, passing a short overhanging bulge and entering a large depression. Simulclimbing leads up and left out of the depression to the left-center portion of the south face and eventually the summit.
gear: Two 60-meter ropes (double-rope rappels on the north-side descent)
Pitons or stoppers for marginal protection
fa: Jens Klubberud and Ben Manfredi, July 2001
